# Introduction

<!-- Rubric 20%: research and analyse the problem. Back every claim with a citation or own test. -->

Autonomous navigation is a core capability of mobile robots: the robot must sense
its surroundings, decide where to go and act on that decision in a closed loop
[@benari2018elements; @corke2023robotics]. Maze solving is a classic, well-defined
version of this problem. [Add 2-3 sentences on why mazes are a useful test case and
which known strategies exist, with citations.]

## Problem statement

The task is to program an iRobot Create 3 so that it drives autonomously from a
start point to a finish point through a maze it has not seen before. The maze has a
flat floor and walls at approximately 90° to each other, and it may contain loops.
The start and finish are revealed only minutes before the demonstration.

<!-- Make the research question specific and measurable, never just "best". Example: -->
This leads to the following research question: *[Which of the two controllers,
A or B, reaches the finish more often and in less time in a previously unseen maze
with loops?]*

## System description

The platform consists of the components listed in @tbl-hardware. The Create 3
publishes its sensor data and receives velocity commands over ROS 2
[@macenski2022ros2; @create3docs]. Our control software runs as a Python node on
the Raspberry Pi.

::: {#tbl-hardware layout-ncol=1}
| Component | Model / version | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile base | iRobot Create 3 | wheels, 7 IR proximity sensors, bumpers, odometry |
| Computer | Raspberry Pi 4 | runs our control node |
| LiDAR | Slamtec RPLiDAR A1M8 | 360° distance measurement [@rplidara1] |
| Operating system | Ubuntu 24.04 | |
| Middleware | ROS 2 Jazzy, Cyclone DDS | communication between nodes |
| Language | Python [version] | control program |

Hardware and software used.
:::

The seven IR sensors return a dimensionless reflection intensity; a larger value
means a closer obstacle. They are fused into three directions: *front* is the
maximum of the four front sensors, *left* is the maximum of the two left sensors
(side_left and left), and *right* is the single right sensor. The maximum is used
because the closest wall in a direction determines the robot's reaction.

# Design

<!-- Rubric 25%: design a solution; compare at least 2 designs WITH literature for an 8. -->

## Design A: reactive priority controller

The first design is purely reactive: at 10 Hz it reads the latest IR values and
applies four rules in priority order (@tbl-reactive). It keeps no memory of earlier
decisions.

::: {#tbl-reactive layout-ncol=1}
| Priority | Condition | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $front > 300$ | stop, rotate towards the more open side |
| 2 | $left > 200$ | drive forward, steer right |
| 3 | $right > 200$ | drive forward, steer left |
| 4 | otherwise | drive straight |

Rules of the reactive controller (Design A).
:::

## Design B: left-hand wall follower as a finite-state machine

The second design implements the left-hand rule [@benari2018elements]: by keeping a
wall on its left, the robot eventually reaches an exit that is connected to the
outer wall. Behaviour is organised as a finite-state machine with the states
FIND_WALL, FOLLOW_WALL, TURN_RIGHT, TURN_LEFT and BACK_UP. Hysteresis
($front > 300$ to start turning, $front < 150$ to stop) prevents oscillation, and a
proportional controller keeps a constant distance to the left wall:

$$
\omega = -K_p \,(left - left_{target})
$$ {#eq-pcontrol}

where $\omega$ is the angular velocity (rad/s) and $K_p$ the proportional gain.

## Validation experiments

Each design was tested on the following sequence: a single straight wall, an inside
corner, an outside corner, and a complete test maze. For each run we recorded
whether the robot reached the finish, the completion time (s) and the number of
bumper contacts. [Describe the test maze: size in m, layout, number of loops.]
